devotionals.theme: COPING WITH BEREAVEMENT
devotionals.themeIntroduction: Continued from the last issue
devotionals.text: “Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.” – Isaiah 41:10.
devotionals.comment:
Grief can bring about feelings of fear and uncertainty about the future. However, God has promised to be with all those that put their trust in Him during times of fear and difficulty.

“God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea.” (Psalm 46:1, 2) The Psalmist also declared: “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.” (Psalm 23:4)

Therefore, we should put our trust in God Almighty in whatever situation we find ourselves. “Trust ye in the LORD for ever: for in the LORD JEHOVAH is everlasting strength.” – Isaiah 26:4.

devotionals.theme: COPING WITH BEREAVEMENT
devotionals.themeIntroduction: Continued from the last issue
devotionals.text: “Cast not away therefore your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward. For ye have need of patience, that, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise.” – Hebrews 10:35,36.
devotionals.comment:
This verse is a message of hope and encouragement to all going through difficult times, not to be discouraged, but to be patient, resilient and to have faith in God that brighter days will come.

St. Paul further states: “Now the just shall live by faith: but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him. But we are not of them who draw back unto perdition; but of them that believe to the saving of the soul.” (Hebrews 10:38,39)

James, the apostle, also encouraged Christians to exercise patience in times of difficulties: “Blessed is the man that endureth temptation: for when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life, which the Lord hath promised to them that love him.” – James 1:12. See also Hebrews 12:1,2; 1 Corinthians 15:58.

devotionals.theme: COPING WITH BEREAVEMENT
devotionals.themeIntroduction: Continued from the last issue
devotionals.text: “But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope.” – 1 Thessalonians 4:13.
devotionals.comment:
This verse encourages Christians to comfort one another with the hope of resurrection and eternal life by God's grace. When facing loss, believers can find solace in the knowledge that death is a temporary state, since they will be reunited with their loved ones in God's Kingdom fully set up by the grace of God. (Job 19:25,26; Daniel 12:2; John 5:28,29)

“For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's.” (Romans 14:8) With this assurance of resurrection, Christians can live with confidence, joy and peace, knowing that their hope extends beyond this life.

It was St. Paul who declared: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable.” – 1 Corinthians 15:19.

devotionals.theme: COPING WITH BEREAVEMENT
devotionals.themeIntroduction: Continued from the last issue
devotionals.text: “Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him.” – Job 13:15.
devotionals.comment:
This text is a great declaration of unwavering faith in the Almighty God even in the face of extreme adversity. It shows Job's deep trust in God's goodness and sovereignty even after he suffered significant losses to his estate and family. (Job 1:13-20)

But he maintained his integrity, trust and confidence in God and declared: “...till I die I will not remove mine integrity from me.” (Job 27:5) Job demonstrated that one way to cope with bereavement and adversity is to have strong belief and trust in God Almighty.

“The LORD also will be a refuge for the oppressed, a refuge in times of trouble. And they that know thy name will put their trust in thee: for thou, LORD, hast not forsaken them that seek thee.” – Psalms 9:9,10.

devotionals.theme: COPING WITH BEREAVEMENT
devotionals.themeIntroduction: Continued from the last issue
devotionals.text: “Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.” – Acts 14:22.
devotionals.comment:
Paul and Barnabas strengthened the faith of the disciples by encouraging them to persevere in their faith amid trials and tribulations as entering the Kingdom of God requires facing difficulties, bereavements and persecutions. (2 Timothy 3:12)

A clear understanding of this reality will enable Christians to cope with any form of trials, tribulations, afflictions including bereavements. This verse directly indicates that the reality of suffering is not only a necessary part of a Christian's life but also assures believers that perseverance will lead to the ultimate reward. (Matthew 24:12,13; 1 Thessalonians 3:3-5)

Christians are reminded that difficulties and challenges are not unexpected and should be met with persistence and reliance on God's strength. See James 1:2-4.

devotionals.theme: COPING WITH BEREAVEMENT
devotionals.themeIntroduction: Continued from the last issue
devotionals.text: “Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.” – Matthew 5:4.
devotionals.comment:
The promise that those who mourn will be comforted can be a significant source of hope and strength to those dealing with the loss of a beloved one. Embedded in his sermon on the mount, is the second of the Beatitudes that forms the main text for today.

In 2 Corinthians 1:3, 4, it is written: “Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort; Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.”

The Psalmist also declared: “The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit. Furthermore, he stated: “Many are the afflictions of the righteous but the LORD delivereth him out of them all.” – Psalm 34:18,19. See also Psalm 145:18-20.

devotionals.theme: CONTRITION
devotionals.themeIntroduction: The statement of David the King in Psalm 51:5, “Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me” or of the Patriarch Job in Job 14:4, “Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean not one” is no justification for one to take pleasure in godlessness. Both texts, instead, express man's frailty and susceptibility to sin. This notwithstanding, a worshipper of God who is sincerely desirous of attaining perfection, readily shows remorse, upon realisation of his error. Contrition, therefore, is a state of being contrite or genuinely remorseful of wrongdoing. As a virtue, it earns one God's forgiveness, and blessings by His grace. We shall in the following days consider the spiritual benefits of contrition by God's grace.
devotionals.text: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” – 1 John 1:8,9.
devotionals.comment:
One can only be remorseful if he has accepted his error, otherwise, such contrition may either be hypocritical, or done under duress or coercion, which in either case, will not attract God's forgiveness.

The servant of God, Job made the declaration: “If I covered my transgressions as Adam, by hiding mine iniquity in my bosom: what then shall I do when God riseth up? And when he visiteth, what shall I answer him?” “Is not destruction to the wicked? and a strange punishment to the workers of iniquity? Doth not he see my ways, and count all my steps?” (Job 31:33,14,3,4)

Therefore, when we are humble enough to receive chastisement, “afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.” – Hebrews 12:11. See also 2 Corinthians 7:9,10.

devotionals.text: “Then he sheweth them their work, and their transgressions that they have exceeded. He openeth also their ear to discipline, and commandeth that they return from iniquity.” – Job 36:9,10.
devotionals.comment:
In exercise of His unfailing mercies, God Almighty is not willing that any should perish “but that all should come to repentance”. (2 Peter 3:9; Ezekiel 18:30-32; 33:11) Saul was one of those who had his error pointed out to him but blew the opportunity by being insincere in his repentance. (1 Samuel 15:24, 30)

Not only did Saul attempt to offer justification by blaming his presumptuousness on the people, but it is also evident that he cared more about his reputation, rather than showing penance. In contrast, we should emulate the approach of David, in the matter of Uriah's wife, and not allow our ego to prevent us from gaining God's mercy. (2 Samuel 12:13)

“If ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land: But if ye refuse and rebel, ye shall be devoured with the sword: for the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it.” – Isaiah 1:19,20. See also Job 36:11,12.

devotionals.text: “He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsakess them shall have mercy.” – Proverbs 28:13.
devotionals.comment:
Some people fail to realise that “all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.” (Hebrews 4:13) Due to lack of the fear of God, they brazenly indulge in acts that violate God's laws, hoping they will get away with it.

The example of Cain who tried to cover the gruesome murder of Abel his brother, (Genesis 4:8-15) and that of Ananias and Sapphira who tried to hide their treachery (Acts 5:1-11), should serve as a lesson to the children of God.

Thus, it is evident that confessing and forsaking our sins are essentials in our obtaining God's forgiveness and mercy by His grace. “Happy is the man that feareth alway: but he that hardeneth his heart shall fall into mischief.” – Proverbs 28:14.

devotionals.text: “He looketh upon men, and if any say, I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it profited me not; He will deliver his soul from going into the pit, and his life shall see the light.” – Job 33:27,28.
devotionals.comment:
The point has often been made that the door of salvation is open to the gentiles, and accommodating to all shades of character, on the condition of their own willingness and readiness to fully forsake their old ways, “cease to do evil,” and “Learn to do well,” in that, God's high way, being regimented, abhors “all appearance of evil.” (1 Thessalonians 5:22)

To remain in God's way of holiness and relish in works of the flesh, is not only an act of ingratitude, but an affront, for which, in God's appointed time, such ones shall be punished according to their works. (2 Corinthians 5:10)

God's word, intrinsically, cleanses, sanctifies, purges, propels a feeling of guilt in one and inspires one to make a resolution to forsake sin, especially when one acknowledges that the words are divinely inspired.” – John 15:3; 17:17; Psalm 119:7-9.

devotionals.text: “Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil; if ye be willing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land.” – Isaiah 1:16,19.
devotionals.comment:
Writing on God's mercy to both forgive and accept even the worst sinner, Isaiah the prophet added: “…though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.” (Isaiah 1:18)

Such pardon is preceded by the individual's willingness to reject and condemn the sin. The person should realise the wrongness of the act and accept the sanctifying effect of God's word, with a firm resolution and determination never to commit such sins again. This, the Bible terms “godly sorrow” in 2 Corinthians 7:9,10.

Today's devotional is therefore a call to action for all and sundry to have a contrite heart. “…but to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word.” – Isaiah 66:2; 57:15.

devotionals.text: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.” – Psalm 51:17.
devotionals.comment:
“Broken spirit” means to be overwhelmed with sorrow, while a “contrite heart” is one that is completely penitent, feeling remorseful, affected by guilt, deeply regretful and willing to atone for one's sin.

Rather than allowing one's sinful commitment instil a sense of regret and feeling of disappointment in one, the devil makes one to become more concerned about the “damage”, corrections or rebuke will do to one's reputation, or the goodwill such person stand to lose from their admirers, when one is exposed, causing such person to go on the defensive by justifying one's actions, or by outright denial, or even going to any length to pervert the course of justice, forgetting that the judgment of God is inescapable. – 2 Corinthians 5:10; Ecclesiastes 12:13,14; 1 Corinthians 11:32.

devotionals.text: “For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death. For though I made you sorry with a letter, I do not repent, though I did repent: for I perceive that the same epistle hath made you sorry, though it were but for a season.” – 2 Corinthians 7:10,8.
devotionals.comment:
In drawing a contrast between godly and worldly sorrow, it would seem as if the erudite apostle was contradicting himself, but this was not the case. St. Paul had initially expressed his unreserved condemnation over certain misdeeds of the Corinthian converts through a previous letter which caused a moment of unease and distress.

This feeling of sorrow or regret over their action moved Paul greatly, even to the point of feeling sorry for them, and not that he regretted the content of his letter.

This is better understood in his epistle to the Hebrew believers, when he wrote: “For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.” – Hebrews 12:6,11.

devotionals.text: “Lest strangers be filled with thy wealth; and thy labours be in the house of a stranger; And thou mourn at the last, when thy flesh and thy body are consumed, And say, How have I hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof; And have not obeyed the voice of my teachers, nor inclined mine ear to them that instructed me!” – Proverbs 5:10-13.
devotionals.comment:
Pondering on the regrets, anguish, embarrassment or shame that come along with sin, it is better to avoid sin at all cost, God being our help. True, the Almighty God takes delight when we acknowledge our errors and repent of them.

The fact is, certain errors are avoidable, where we allow God's ordinances to always be our guide. The Prophet Samuel told Saul, “…Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.” (1 Samuel 15:22-26).

Today's leading text is specific on the vice of adultery, which unfortunately, a good number of persons continue to swim in, secretly and openly in some cases (Proverbs 6:24-35). It therefore requires sincere and steadfast commitment to the above resolve, for one to avoid regret in the end, all by God's grace. – See Job 31:1,3,9,10.

devotionals.text: “So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them, And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he could do unto them; and he did it not.” – Jonah 3:5,10.
devotionals.comment:
The beauty in serving God, among others, lies in the fact that, He is ever forgiven, and His mercy endures forever. (Psalm 107:1) Today's devotional calls to mind, the impressive turnaround of an entire city numbering over 120,000 persons, occasioned by the warning from God Almighty through His servant, Jonah.

Worth commending, is the approach of the unnamed king who led the entire city to true repentance for which God showed them mercy as highlighted in the leading text. (Jonah 3:6-9)

God's forgiveness on the people of Nineveh, amplifies the words of the Prophet Isaiah to wit: “Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near. Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.” – Isaiah 55:6,7.

devotionals.text: “And he spake this parable unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others…for every one that exalted himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.” – Luke 18:9,14.
devotionals.comment:
In his usual manner of conveying his messages by means of parables, Jesus Christ drives home the point on humility and sincerity in acknowledging one's frailty and confessing one's error respectively, using two men, one a Pharisee, the other a publican, who both went into the temple to pray.

While the Pharisee justified himself by referencing his tithe payment, fasting, and abstinence from sin, which distinguished him from others, the publican, “standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.” In Christ's justified assessment, “this man went down to his house justified rather than the other”. (Luke 18:9-14)

It could be seen therefore, that a contrite and penitent heart is devoid of arrogance and an over-estimation of one's worth. – 1 Peter 5:6.

devotionals.text: “Before I was afflicted I went astray: but now have I kept thy word. It is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes.” – Psalm 119:67,71.
devotionals.comment:
No discourse on contrition can be said to be exhaustive without reference to a man who earned the reputation of being designated a man after God's heart, one known for his consistency in admitting his error and seeking God's forgiveness, without offering justification for his misdeed.

He, David, had earlier declared: “The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.” (Psalm 34:18) As against the practice of blaming others for one's misfortune or accusing God Almighty of forsaking one, David would rather trace his affliction to his own error or misdeed as captured in Psalm 119:67. See also Lamentations 3:39,40.

Turning to the Almighty God entails praying to gain His forgiveness, meditating on His precepts which confer spiritual enlightenment on His children, and ensuring to “do according to all that is written therein” by His grace. – Joshua 1:8.

devotionals.text: “I thought on my ways, and turned my feet unto thy testimonies. I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments.” – Psalm 119:59,60.
devotionals.comment:
Oftentimes, sin puts a gulf between God Almighty and His children, making Him to remove His protection from us, and paving way for our chief adversary, the Devil, to buffet us. (Isaiah 59:1,2; Psalm 107:17) We offend in many ways (James 3:2) through the thoughts of our heart, our utterances, what we look at, what we do with our bodies and so on.

We can ascertain our moral status before our Maker, when we cultivate the habit of reflecting on our ways, (2 Corinthians 13:5,6) King David declared: “I call to remembrance my song in the night: I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search.” (Psalm 77:6; 4:4; 1 Corinthians 11:31)

When such self-reappraisal is done in sincerity, using God's statutes for a guide, we will be able to identify areas where we have fallen short. The next step should be to confess and forsake such, with prayer to God Almighty for the grace and strength to live true to our resolve by His grace. See Job 34:31,32.

devotionals.text: “For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the hearts.” – Hebrews 4:12.
devotionals.comment:
The indicting, invasive, and sanctifying effect of God's precept were all demonstrated during the event that played out on the day of Pentecost.

It happened that, after St. Peter's captivating expository on the greatness, authority and messiahship of Jesus Christ, “…they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, men and brethren, what shall we do?” (Acts 2:37) The foregoing authenticates Paul the apostle's designation of the word of God as “words of truth and soberness.” (Acts 26:25)

It either indicts or excuses us when we err or when we do well, respectively. Contrition as a virtue, therefore, begins with one's readiness and humility to hear and submit oneself to God's word. – Psalm 85:8.

There was a time Hezekiah, King of Judah was “sick unto death”, and God Almighty instructed His servant, Isaiah to inform him thus, “set thine house in order: for thou shalt die, and not live.” When he heard this stark judgement of God, he was naturally frightful and sorrowful.

Turning to God in prayer, he besought the Most High “Remember now, O LORD, I beseech thee, how I have walked before thee in truth and good things that he had done over the years. The Ever Merciful Father turned from His position and miraculously healed him, and added unto his days fifteen years. (Isaiah 38:5)

In a show of gratitude, he expressed his determination to live a life of sobriety. Because at death, none would be able to praise God, he vowed to praise His Maker while he had his breath. (Isaiah 38:18,19)

It follows therefore that, having acknowledged one's sin, and confessed same; there should be a conscious resolve to live a life of holiness. – Micah 6:8; John 8:11; 1 Thessalonians 5:22; Ezekiel 18:24.

devotionals.comment:
St. Paul admonishes that nothing should be done out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, but in humility we should consider others better than ourselves. In all our endeavours, we are expected to look not only to our interests, but also to the interests of others. Our attitude should be the same as that of Christ Jesus. (Philippians 2:3-5; Matthew 7:12; Romans 13:8)

Today, selfish ambitions are often greatly applauded, while such persons live to glorify themselves with untamed pursuit for personal interest and gratification at the detriment of others. Those who have the fear of God must desist from such bad, inordinate behaviour, which yields bitter fruits in the long run.

The Scriptures prescribe the use of prayer, supplication, and thanksgiving as a sure recipe for achieving our godly ambitions. See Philippians 4:6,7.

devotionals.comment:
There seems to be a generational erosion of the understanding that there is dignity in labour. Instead, the trend has become “get-rich” by any means, largely due to a society that reveres the wealthy, regardless of the source of their wealth.

This sort of get-rich ambition is exhibited by many young people, including teenagers, in our society nowadays. To compound the problem, some parents do not bother to ask their children about the source of their wealth, even with the knowledge that the children are still in school or unemployed.

Thus, the love of money has led many to indulge in heinous crimes such as ritual killings and occult practices. Others engage in violent armed robbery, kidnapping for ransom, internet fee fraud, embezzlement, etc., without any shred of conscience.

“A faithful man shall abound with blessings: but he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent. He that hasteth to be rich hath an evil eye, and considereth not that poverty shall come upon him.” – Proverbs 28:20,22.

To achieve his evil intentions, Absalom spoke evil of his father, David, to all who came to Jerusalem for justice. He used every trick in the book, such as innuendos, insinuations, ingratiation, kissing, handshakes, backslapping, flattery, and commiseration, to promote himself and to put his father, King David, down.

However, there was only one problem: it was not God's will for Absalom to be king, and he lost his life in an inglorious manner as indicated in the leading text.

A selfishly ambitious person wants very much to achieve that which God denies. Promotion comes from God alone. – Psalm 75:6,7; 1 Peter 5:6.

Korah was a Levite who had a very good responsibility of transporting the furniture of God's tabernacle, but he was not satisfied with God's calling for him. This was why Samuel the prophet, in a “conscience void of offence towards God and man”, made his valedictory speech to the Israelites, who responded positively in his favour, to the glory of God. (1 Samuel 12:1-5)

Jezebel, bereft of the knowledge of God's standards, could not provide her husband with godly counsel, instead she became the source of catastrophe to Ahab's lineage. She devised a devilish plan to murder Naboth and covet his inheritance for her husband, the King. (1 Kings 21:15,16)

Saul, during his reign as King of Israel, desired to also perform the duties of a king and a priest in the Lord's temple, notwithstanding the fact that Samuel had been anointed by God to fulfil that duty.

Eventually, he lost his place as the Lord's chosen, and the spirit of God departed from Him. (1 Samuel 16:14,15) In reality, it was Satan who troubled Saul when God's spirit departed from him. This led a once promising young King of Israel to a downward spiral into idolatry, envy, infamy, and eventual ignominious death.

The lesson from Saul's story is that children of God should endeavour to align their ambitions to God's will for mankind. Anything contrary amounts to selfish ambition, whose end is always unprofitable to the individual. – Ephesians 6:6-8.

Uzziah was presumptuous when he became established on the throne. “But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the LORD his God, and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense.” (2 Chronicles 26:16)

The Psalmist declared: “Correction is grievous unto him that forsaketh the way: and he that hateth reproof shall die.” (Proverbs 15:10) Let us always recall the prayer of King David in all we do, “Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer.” – Psalm 19:14.

For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north: I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High.” – Isaiah 14:12-14.
devotionals.comment:
The tragedy that eventually befalls those who are selfishly ambitious is vividly seen with what happened to Lucifer, who at his prime was one of the angels of God until inordinate ambition led to his downfall. He was not satisfied with his high office. He wanted more than what God had provided for him. He wanted to be like God himself.

“…Thine heart was lifted up because of thy beauty, thou hast corrupted thy wisdom by reason of thy brightness: I will cast thee to the ground, I will lay thee before kings, that they may behold thee...” (Ezekiel 28:12-19)

We should not allow our gifts or talents lead us into ungodly ambition as it did to Lucifer, who lost his glory, position and name, no longer Lucifer, but now known as Satan, Serpent, Devil and Dragon. – Revelation 12:9. See also 1 Peter 5:6.

devotionals.text: “For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south. But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another.” – Psalms 75:6,7.
devotionals.comment: God Almighty owns the prerogative for helping His obedient children achieve their godly ambitions that are in accordance with His will. So was the case with Joseph, and so many other righteous men and women of Bible fame. Even when faced with obstacles, alluring temptations, and other forces that could have derailed their efforts to achieve their ambitions, they remained firm, working within the bounds of God's laws. Joseph endured being sold into slavery, resisted his master's wife's tempting immoral offer, false accusation, served time in prison, but was eventually elevated by the LORD to be a ruler in a foreign land. (Acts 7:9,10) Similarly, Daniel defied the threat of death by choosing to hold fast to his faith and was eventually made a ruler in Babylon. (Daniel 6:25-28) These and other examples recorded in the Holy Writ serve as a veritable testament of God's assured blessings, promotion, and salvation to all who remain steadfast in the practice of His righteousness. See Psalms 37:4,34-40; Joshua 1:8; Philippians 4:19; Matthew 23:12.

devotionals.themeIntroduction: Continued from the last issue
devotionals.text: “We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let every one of us please his neighbour for his good to edification. For even Christ pleased not himself; but, as it is written, The reproaches of them that reproached thee fell on me.” – Romans 15:1-3.
devotionals.comment:
For us to overcome selfish and inordinate ambition, we are required to cultivate humility, prioritize others' needs over our own, practise gratitude, listen actively, and commit to selfless acts of service and compassion. We can also find guidance in the Scriptures by drawing lessons from biblical example. If we do this with an honest heart, it will help to shift our focus from getting immersed in the pursuit of personal gain to contributing to something larger than ourselves. Scriptures admonish that we should take the time to understand and care about the needs and goals of the people around us.

We should aim to be “givers” rather than “receivers,” focusing on how we can contribute to the well-being of others. When we imbibe the virtue of service, we can then eradicate the thoughts that fuel selfish ambition. See Galatians 5:13-17.

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “And herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men.” – Acts 24:16
devotionals.comment:
Without faith, it is impossible to please the Almighty God. (Hebrews 11:6) But coupled with faith, we must also have a good conscience, firstly a conscience void of offense towards God and then towards men. (Acts 24:16). A good conscience safeguards Christian faith and life. Faith and a good conscience go together. Whenever there is an offence in our conscience, there will be a leakage, and our faith will dwindle away.

Wherever we find ourselves, we must demonstrate that we have a good conscience by being honest with people. We should prove our integrity just like apostle Paul told the Jewish leaders when he was arraigned before them. He boldly told them: “Men and brethren, I have lived in all good conscience before God until this day.” – Acts 23:1

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “Holding faith, and a good conscience; which some having put away concerning faith have made ship wreck.” – 1 Timothy 1:19.
devotionals.comment: If we are careless in matters of faith and a good conscience, we can gradually develop an evil heart of unbelief (one that has lost faith). These can make us fall away from God. (Hebrews 3:12) To preserve us from such a falling away, we are told to exhort and encourage one another every day. Apostle Paul exhorted the Hebrew converts which applies to us today when he said: “But exhort one another daily, while it is called today; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. (Hebrews 3:13) In the text under reference, apostle Paul mentioned Hymenaeus and Alexander who had lost their faith in the service of God, backslided and blasphemed. (1 Timothy 1:20) Losing faith and hope in the worship of God leads to “shipwreck of faith “and complete ruin of one's salvation unless there is a retrace of steps. May God make our faith strong in Him and in His divine work.

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things. Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God.” – 1 John 3:20,21.
devotionals.comment: The leading text addresses the worshipper's conscience in the service of God. It gives an assurance that even if the heart condemns us for sin, God's judgment is supreme and His knowledge is complete. As worshippers of God, we are encouraged to live right with God so that our hearts do not condemn us wrongly. Our outward behaviour, particularly love for one another, should prove us to our neighbours that a clean conscience comes from a sincere effort to live according to God's will. That “God is greater than our heart, and knows all things” means God is not limited by our own feelings or human limitations. He knows completely our intentions and the full context of our actions, and His judgment is the final. If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God. This means that when we are living in obedience, we can approach God with greater boldness and assurance in our prayers.

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “Having a good conscience; that, whereas they speak evil of you, as of evil doers, they may be ashamed that falsely accuse your good conversation in Christ.” – 1 Peter 3:16.
devotionals.comment: We must be careful to always preserve the sensitivity of our consciences. A disturbed conscience implies that we have left the safe ‘channel' and are in turbulent waters. We must ignore people who speak evil of us for no just cause. Ignoring the signs of a wrong conscience could plunge one into “shipwreck”. If we maintain our implicit faith in God, if we are buffeted for doing what is right, we should take it joyfully like the apostles of old. Even though they were tortured they counted themselves as conquerors. Hence Apostle Peter admonished: “For it is better, if the will of God be so, that ye suffer for well doing than for evil doing. (1 Peter 3:17) It takes great faith to endure this admonition.

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “Then said Jesus unto the twelve, Will ye also go away? Then Simon Peter answered him, Lord, to whom shall we go? Thou hast the words of eternal life.” – John 6:67,68.
devotionals.comment: St. Peter was a steadfast follower of Jesus Christ, his master. He was quick to respond to questions asked by the Lord. Peter's faith and hope in Christ as the Lord and Saviour was not in doubt. In the opening text for today, Jesus was questioning the twelve after he made some figurative statements that offended some of his disciples. A lack of understanding of his statement made some of them lose faith and hope in him. He told them that he was the “bread of life”. (verse 48) Going further, he said that “…Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.” “Many therefore of his disciples, when they had heard this, said, This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. (verse 60) This was what prompted Jesus Christ to ask his immediate 12 disciples as in the text for today. In the Church today, many worshippers do not like judgment. They hate corrections and rebuke when they have done wrong. They easily get offended and withdraw themselves from responsibilities given to them to execute. They are not hopeful and become faithless. This should not be so with us. – Colossians 2:6,7.

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “May the God of your hope so fill you with all joy and peace in believing [through the experience of your faith] that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound and be overflowing (bubbling over) with hope.” – Romans 15:13 (AMP)
devotionals.comment: St. Paul in his supplications for the early Roman Christian converts talks about what God Almighty could do in the hearts of His faithful worshippers. JEHOVAH is a God of hope. One, Who is the only lasting source of hope that men must have for a meaningful life in this wicked world of sin. This hope goes beyond this world of distress and perplexity to the world without end where man who is faithful and righteous in the sight of God has the hope of eternal life. As worshippers who trust in the Living God, our faith would radiate joy and bring peace to our hearts. This hope and faith will make us keep believing in the sure mercies of God and His promises for us to experience joy and peace. Isaiah the prophet in this light declared: “Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee because he trusteth in thee. Trust ye in the LORD forever, for in the LORD JEHOVAH is everlasting strength.” – Isaiah 26:3,4.

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience.” – 1 Timothy 3:9.
devotionals.comment: The opening text informs us that as aspiring leaders in God's holy organisation, we must uphold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience, void of offence towards God and towards men. (Acts 24:16) We must uphold the core Christian principles and live practical lives consistent with them. One who is a leader must not pretend. Having a clear conscience is a demonstration of our spiritual life and public life which must synchronise or harmonise, and we must be like our master, Jesus Christ. (Matthew 10:25) God Almighty reveals His mysteries to His anointed ones through Jesus Christ (Deuteronomy 29:29) by which they preach His true doctrines, which was hidden but has been revealed through Jesus Christ. (Ephesians 3:9) Having a clear conscience requires us not to be guilty of lying or pretence but must be authenticated by good works and actions in our services to the Almighty God.

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “For if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning.” – 2 Peter 2:20.
devotionals.comment: This text warns us that have known the truth not to have a superficial or non-genuine association with our worship for God. Having an understanding of the truth, we should continue with hope and faith in God, so that we do not fall away. For those that have the truth and fall away, their end is worse because they have experienced the truth and rejected it. They have returned to their own vomit and they will not have reward at the end. Jeremiah, the prophet said that we should not weep for the dead. But we should weep for those who fall away because they will not see their native land. (Jeremiah 22:10) In rendering services to the Almighty God by our sincere worship we must do so with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water. – Hebrews 10:22.

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “Why art thou cast down, O my soul? And why art thou disquieted within me? Hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.” – Psalms 42:11.
devotionals.comment: How do we as worshippers of God go through trials? What do we do when everything seems to be going wrong, or even when everything is going right, but we feel miserable? What do we do when we are discouraged? These are questions that bother us in our daily lives, and they have been so for ages. Men who gave themselves to the practice of righteousness who we consider very spiritual also ask these questions when they face trials. King David was one of such men. When we think of David, we typically think of David as a man of War or a king who was a sweet Psalmist, the young ruddy boy who killed Goliath. But he had his troubles. After his adulterous act with Bathsheba, trouble sprang from his house through his son, Absalom. In his troubles he hoped in the God of Mercy hence his statement in the leading text for today. This hope is not based on his own strength, but on the reliability and promises of God. This should be the assurance for all who hope in the LORD.

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “The peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and…minds in Christ Jesus.” – Philippians 4:7 (NIV).
devotionals.comment: No matter what problems we are grappling with, it is good to know that the peace of God “which transcends all understanding, will guard our hearts and…minds in Christ Jesus.” Do we find ourselves in difficult situations that affect our lives? Are we looking for wives, husbands, children, jobs? Do we have a large family that we cannot take care of? Do we live in a house that is not ours and we find it difficult to pay rent? These are questions that fog our minds like suffocating smoke. When these life problems arise, our natural inclination is to panic. When we do that, we open the door for the Enemy to come in, get us off track, and make us feel victimised. What we need is to look to God with faith and hope that He is able to make things right. When we have this disposition, we have the peace of mind without any worries. This was the admonition of Christ in John 14:27. Hope in God and serving Him in good conscience will bring us out of despair.

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “The Lord God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places…” – Habakkuk 3:19.
devotionals.comment: Habakkuk expresses faith in the Living God despite a future challenge he may face. This is also what we as worshippers of God should do. The opening text enjoins us of a transformation from having doubts to having implicit trust or faith in God in the most difficult situations. Without this faith, no man can please Him. (Hebrews 11:6) We live in hope and walk by faith in difficult times. The present situation we find ourselves in the world today where there is banditry, kidnappings, terrorism, herdsmen/farmers' clashes call for great faith in God for deliverance especially in the most troubled spots. Apostle Paul rightly admonished: “We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed.” (2 Corinthians 4:8,9) As worshippers of God, we should have hope, strength, agility and spiritual elevation to encourage us to trust in the Almighty God to support us in difficult and challenging circumstances. – Psalms 37:23,24.

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “Now this is our boast: Our conscience testifies that we have conducted ourselves in the world, and especially in our relations with you, with integrity and godly sincerity. We have done so, relying not on worldly wisdom but on God's grace.” – 2 Corinthians 1:12 (NIV).
devotionals.comment: The leading text encourages us to conduct ourselves with godly sincerity and holiness and not on fleshly or human wisdom. In all our actions, we must be guided by divine sincerity and the grace of God. We could like St. Paul, have a boast of a good conscience void of offence towards God and towards men. (Acts 24:16) Having a good conscience in serving God will help us to behave in an honourable manner especially among the wicked of this world. As people in the truth and walking in the way of holiness, we must have confrontational relationship with our families who are not in the true way and those who are in the broad way because of our beliefs that are contrary to their ways. We must avoid inappropriate behaviours in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation we find ourselves so that we can win them to God just like what St. Peter admonished godly wives to be submissive to their husbands so that if any (of the ungodly women) obey not the word, they might be won by the conversation (good conduct) of the wives while they behold their chaste conversation coupled with the fear of God in them. – 1 Peter 3:1-3.

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.” – Hebrews 10:22.
devotionals.comment: We have days where we feel we cannot survive. Sometimes dreams are shattered, friendships may fall apart, loved ones may hurt us, finances may worry us and sickness may overtake us. But JEHOVAH, the Almighty God will not forsake us but will always be there for us to guide us through the toughest of times. We should never lose hope and faith in God Almighty. We should hold on to hope and have good conscience. As the devotional of today explains, we must draw close to God Almighty, our Creator with an unqualified assurance and absolute conviction of implicit faith and have a purified conscience unlike the wicked who have consciences seared with “hot” iron. (1 Timothy 4:2) We should not draw back from God and His work but be diligent in His service for a full reward at the end by His grace.

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “Now the just shall live by faith: but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him.” – Hebrews 10:38.
devotionals.comment:
Faith keeps our eyes on the rich promises of God while a good conscience keeps our hearts clean and clear before Him. When we have a good conscience, it helps our faith to work for God because like James, the apostle, and brother of our Lord Jesus Christ said, “Faith without works is dead.” When we have a clear conscience and know that we are right with God, it's easier for us to believe and trust God.

We must never lose our total confidence in God and draw back or backslide.

We must have strong confidence in our Creator. That is what it means to live by faith. Unfortunately, the phrase “living by faith” has been changed by some to refer to God providing money for their needs. This is not correct. The Bible says that “the just shall live by faith” (Romans 1:17). Those who are in the path of righteousness must exercise strong faith and confidence in God at all times. If we are careless in the matters of faith and a good conscience, we can gradually develop an evil heart (a bad conscience) and an unbelieving heart (one that has lost faith). These can make us fall away from the True Way. God forbid!

devotionals.theme: HOLDING FAITH AND A GOOD CONSCIENCE
devotionals.text: “Of whom is Hymenaeus and Alexander; whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.” – 1 Timothy 1:20.
devotionals.comment: Apparently faith and a good conscience go together and work together. A good conscience is one that is free from guilt whereas an evil conscience is a guilty conscience. Those who have put away faith and good conscience have made shipwreck of their life. They did not just ignore their consciences but rather made great effort to deaden and push away their consciences. The erudite apostle mentioned two apostates, Hymenaeus and Alexander, who abandoned what they once believed or held as doctrine, belief, and principles. These two Paul delivered over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme (2 Timothy 1:20) Can we have a clear conscience? Yes, we can. Let us repent receiving forgiveness and cleansing by confessing our sins (1 John 1:9) The blood of Jesus Christ has the power to cleanse and purge our consciences from all defilement through the preaching of the truth or everlasting gospel of Christ to avoid a shipwreck.

devotionals.theme: BEWARE OF WHAT YOU SOW IN LIFE
devotionals.themeIntroduction:
The word “beware” as defined by good dictionaries means “to be careful”, “to be on one's guard”, “to be circumspect”. To “sow” means to scatter or plant seeds in order to grow crops. In the context of this theme “sow” means to make utterances, take actions and our thoughts which could lead to blessings or punishment in future. Life is the period between birth and death.

“Beware Of What You Sow In Life” is an exhortation and warning for us to be mindful of what we do, say or think in our sojourn in this world so that we do not reap the vengeance of the ungodly and that of God Almighty in the end. It is aimed at guiding our actions, improving our habits and making the most of our lives as we continue to serve God. This theme highlights the nexus between actions and consequences.
devotionals.text: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the spirit shall of the spirit reap life everlasting.” – Galatians 6:7,8.
devotionals.comment: This is a stark reminder of the close connection between causes and effects. It expresses both the principle of retribution and that of the justice of God. It is a clear exposition of the law of cause and effect as to make men especially believers in Christ to be mindful that their new life in Christ is that of stewardship for which they shall give account. We sow by what we do, utter and think. It illustrates the Bible truth that each and every one of us will be rewarded by God according to how we use the opportunity He has given us to come to the truth. St. Paul, the erudite apostle said that God is not mocked because he knew very well that some people are cunning or insincere in the service of God. The fact however, is that such ones are not serving our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly, and by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple. (Romans 16:18). They forget that God sees all that we do from His abode. – Psalm 11:4; Job 34:22.

devotionals.comment: A farmer who sows wheat expects to reap wheat at the time of harvest. Likewise, if he plants potato, he does not expect to harvest rice. We sow by our utterances, thoughts and deeds. In view of this, reasonable, God-fearing people strive to sow good seeds to reap the blessings of God. But for the wicked who refuse to repent before they will receive their full punishment, the consequences of their actions will be telling on them by way of guilty conscience and not enjoying the peace of God. (Isaiah 48:22) The Prophet Jeremiah admonished “Thine own wickedness shall correct thee, and thy backslidings shall reprove thee: know therefore and see that it is an evil thing and bitter, that thou hast forsaken the LORD thy God, and that my fear is not in thee, saith the LORD of hosts. – Jeremiah 2:19.

devotionals.comment: We should realise that the Omniscient God beholds everything done in the entire universe (Psalm 11:4) Nothing is hidden from Him, this understanding should make us endeavour to do things that are pleasing in His sight always. Those who think that the evils they do in secret, God does not see them are deceiving themselves. Achan, a man from the tribe of Judah, disobeyed God's instruction concerning the accursed thing in Joshua 6:18,19, this led to far-reaching consequences, as Israel was defeated by the people of Ai who were fewer in number, when they went to war (Joshua 7:3) Joshua, the prophet did not understand the reason for the defeat until God revealed it to him. Apart from Israel losing the war, Achan's household was stoned to death. (Joshua 8:22-26) Indeed, nothing can be hidden from God Almighty. –Jeremiah 16:17; 2 Chronicles 16:9.

devotionals.comment: This is a reminder that even the thoughts and intents of our hearts are open to our Maker. He is therefore in a position to reward everyone according to his deeds. Owing to human limitations, men are unable to understand the intents of the hearts. God knows the heart and describes it as being “desperately wicked” as it is written: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.” (Jeremiah 17:9,10) The knowledge and realisation of this fact, should make everyone strive to maintain a good heart condition in the service of God. The pureness of our hearts attracts divine blessings. (1 Peter 1:22, Matthew 5:8) But persistence in wrongdoing will lead to destruction. – Proverbs 28:13,14; 29:1.

devotionals.text: “As righteousness tendeth to life: so he that pursueth evil pursueth it to his own death. Though hand join in hand the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered.” – Proverbs 11:19,21.
devotionals.comment: From the above text, it is very clear that man irrespective of his status, will certainly reap what he sows. And there are different ways we sow in this world. We sow by our utterances, actions and thoughts. The Bible contains instances of evil people who committed evils and paid dearly for it. In this regard mention can be made of Haman, the chief minister of King Ahasuerus of Persia, out of hatred for Mordecai, and all the Jews, who in keeping with the laws of God refused to bow down to him, he (Haman) acting on the evil counsel of Zeresh, his wife and friends (Esther 5:10-14) plotted to kill Mordecai, he caused gallows to be built, 50 cubits high. In a nutshell, the plot backfired and he paid dearly for his mischief. (Esther 3:2-6; 7:7-10) Indeed King David did say of the wicked: “Behold he travaileth with iniquity, and hath conceived mischief, and brought forth falsehood. He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made. His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate.” – Psalm 7:14-16; 37:14,15. See also Proverbs 26:24,27; 28:10.

devotionals.comment: Every wicked person knows that he is wicked (Isaiah 59:12). His conscience pricks him when he does evil. He will certainly reap what he sows unless he repents thoroughly to meet the Lord's demand. A few examples will suffice: Jezebel did so much evil during her husband's reign as King of Samaria, though she was not a Jew by birth (1 King 16:30,31) She caused Naboth to be killed, she ruled her husband contrary to divine law (Genesis 3:16) and her husband followed her sheepishly, she encouraged Baal worship in no small way, she even threatened to kill Elijah the Tishbite, a prophet of God for killing the prophets of Baal (1 King 19:1,2) Even when God's judgment was pronounced, Ahab showed contrition, but Jezebel did not, her end was not glorious. (1 Kings 21:23, 24; 2 Kings 9:30-37) Another ready example was Adonibezek, a Canaanite who was rewarded for his cruelty. He was captured and had his thumbs and great toes cut off. Just before his death, he confessed that God had rewarded him as he did to others. – Judges 1:4-7.

And as some wicked people get away with their acts without being detected, perhaps until they die, some think that such ones had escaped God's judgment or that was the end with them. devotionals.comment: The text for today highlights the Bible truth that everyone is answerable to the Creator. Apostle Paul says: “So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.” (Romans 14:12) No one can escape the consequences of his actions. God is no respecter of persons. People who do so are wicked and are aware that their actions hurt others, moreover by so doing, they are sowing bad seeds whose fruits, they shall reap in a determined time, that is as certain as day and night. King Solomon was inspired by God to write: “As righteousness tendeth to life: so he that pursueth evil pursueth it to his own death.” (Proverbs 11:19) Jezebel and Haman are bad examples that should be discarded by serious-minded people. Jezebel conspired to have Naboth killed for refusing to part with his vineyard for Ahab, her husband; while Haman plotted to destroy all the Jews just because Mordecai refused to bow to him. Ahab, Jezebel and Haman all died ignominiously. – Esther 7:1-10; 2 Kings 9:30-37.

devotionals.theme: BEWARE OF WHAT YOU SOW IN LIFE
devotionals.themeIntroduction:
The word “beware” as defined by good dictionaries means “to be careful”, “to be on one's guard”, “to be circumspect”. To “sow” means to scatter or plant seeds in order to grow crops. In the context of this theme “sow” means to make utterances, take actions and our thoughts which could lead to blessings or punishment in future. Life is the period between birth and death.

“Beware Of What You Sow In Life” is an exhortation and warning for us to be mindful of what we do, say or think in our sojourn in this world so that we do not reap the vengeance of the ungodly and that of God Almighty in the end. It is aimed at guiding our actions, improving our habits and making the most of our lives as we continue to serve God. This theme highlights the nexus between actions and consequences.
devotionals.text: “For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister.” – Hebrews 6:10.
devotionals.comment: Unlike fellow mortals who may forget due to human limitations, God remembers all that we do in furtherance of His work and will bless us provided we continue to serve Him faithfully and sincerely in truth and love. For this reason, we should endeavour to sow good seeds, now that the opportunity to do so is still available before it is too late. Mordecai, a Jewish captive in the Kingdom of Persia did something heroic by revealing a plot by two of the king's eunuchs, Bigthana and Teresh, to assassinate the monarch (Esther 2:21-23). But there was no royal acknowledgement for such a heroic act as saving the king's life. But as King Solomon stated: “The King's heart is in the hand of the Lord, as the rivers of water; He turneth it whithersoever he will.” (Proverbs 21:1) One night, the king could not sleep. He called for and had “the book of the records of the chronicles” and discovered that no rewarded has gone to Mordecai. The King later decreed that the royal garments, emblems and mule be used in a parade of honour for Mordecai. – Esther 6:1-11.

devotionals.comment:
The text for today reminds us that there is a day of reckoning, when we shall account for our deeds, even for our utterances we shall account for them. “But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgement.

For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.” (Matthew 12:36,37) The text also shows no one dead or alive can escape the day of reckoning. Therefore, we should endeavour to be sober and mindful of our deeds, utterances and thoughts to ensure they are guided by the spirit of God, in order to be on His side of favour on the day of judgement.

devotionals.comment: Today's text is a stark reminder that actions have consequences. We receive like measure of what we mete to others. devotionals.theme: PASSING THE TIME OF OUR SOJOURNING HERE IN FEAR
devotionals.themeIntroduction: True to scriptural prophecies pointing to the evils of this age, evil men and seducers are intensifying their acts of godlessness to such a disturbing height, with utter disregard for God's laws and human decency. As a peculiar people called to make a difference “in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation”, we are expected to shine as light, Jesus Christ admonishes us to be watchful and prayerful, while Paul the Apostle exhorts us to spiritual circumspection, “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil”. (Luke 21:36; Ephesians 5:15,16) The fear of God, thus, encompasses keeping to His ordinance, (Ecclesiastes 12:13) detaching ourselves from the ungodly and from “all-appearance of evil”. (2 Corinthians 6:14-18; 1 Thessalonians 5:22) All these are achievable through knowledge of God's word.
devotionals.text: “And Moses said unto the people, Fear not: for God is come to prove you, and that his fear may be before your faces, that ye sin not.” – Exodus 20:20.
devotionals.comment:
Two notable points for reflection in today's text are, as against the morbid fear of danger, it is actually our deep, sincere, and uncompromising reverence for God and His statutes, that God Almighty acknowledges and accepts; and also, such reverence for God's ordinance prevents one from sinning against Him, no wonder the Psalmist states: “Thy word have hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.” (Psalm 119:11) Having seen evidence of God's presence among them, when Moses was receiving the Ten Commandments, by way of thunderings, lightnings, and the mountain smoking, “when the people saw it, they removed, and stood afar off. And they said unto Moses, speak thou with us, and we will hear: but let not God speak with us, lest we die” It was in response to this, that Moses made the declaration in verse 20 of Exodus chapter 20.

Under inspiration, the Prophet Isaiah wrote: “Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.” – Isaiah 8:13.

devotionals.text: “Then Peter said unto them, repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost…And with many other words did he testify and exhort, saying, save yourselves from this untoward generation.” – Acts 2:38-40.
devotionals.comment:
Sequel to Peter's defence of his colleagues – the Saints, the exaltation of his Master, Jesus Christ, and the fierce condemnation of the attitude of the unbelieving Jews that when “they heard this, they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, men and brethren, what shall we do?” (verse 37) It was in response to this inquiry that the Apostle made the declaration as captured in the day's leading quote. In continuation, after his preaching, “fear came upon every soul; and many wonders and signs were done by the apostles” (verse 43).

Unfortunately, there are some today who stage opposition to the truth like some people of old: “Now as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth: men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith.” (2 Timothy 3:8) To tremble at God's statutes is to acknowledge that they are divinely inspired. Therefore, frantic efforts should be made to “keep therefore and do them”. The blessing of God awaits all who show genuine reverence for God's laws: “…but to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word.” – Isaiah 66:2.

devotionals.text: “All these things happened to them as examples – as object lessons to us – to warn us against doing the same things; they were written down so that we could read about them and learn from them in these last days as the world nears its end.” – 1 Corinthians 10:11 (The Living Bible).
devotionals.comment:
The impunity with which a good number of the Israelites violated the laws of God, especially in the vices of adultery and fornication, gives one cause for concern. It could be recalled that while they sojourned at Shittim, they defiled themselves with the daughters of Moab, and joined them in their idolatrous acts, for which God Almighty commanded Moses to “Take all the heads of the people, and hang them up before the LORD against the sun….” While Moses was effecting this, amidst the wailing for those who had lost their lives, Zimri brazenly brought in a Midianitish woman, Cozbi, in the sight of Moses, to lay with her. In a show of righteous indignation, Phinehas killed both of them, using a javelin. It was this brave act that made God Almighty to terminate the plague.

Apostle Paul warns Christians: “But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness. Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted…” – 1 Corinthians 10:5,6.

devotionals.text: “And he said unto them, take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.” – Luke 12:15.
devotionals.comment: No doubt, the rapid decline in both spiritual and moral values in an age of distress and peril, places more importance and urgency to St. Paul's admonition in Hebrews 10:25. For instance, the unbridled quest for wealth, even when it is pursued honestly, could itself become a distraction. Spiritual understanding makes it clear that abundance or prosperity are no indices for identifying true worshippers of God, as such notion is a product of a corrupt mind that fails to submit to the truth which is according to godliness, “supposing that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself.” (1 Timothy 6:5) As against Christ's admonition for his followers to give premium to Theocratic interests, the target for some of the ungodly is always to keep acquiring fortunes, to such a degree where one becomes “the talk of the town”. In place of commendation, the sacred volume pronounces curse on such ones, “Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!” (Isaiah 5:8) The point is, our sincere struggle to make ends meet, may become a distraction when it often denies us opportunity to worship our Maker. – Zephaniah 2:1,3.

devotionals.comment: It is most regrettable to observe that the devastation that befell the first world, by way of deluge, both in duration and magnitude, the severity of God's justice on the Israel of old, have still not made the expected impact on the ungodly, instead, “By swearing, and lying and killing and stealing, and committing adultery, they break out, and blood toucheth blood.” (Hosea 4:2) In Eliphaz's words, many “drink iniquity like water” (Job 15:16). They fail to heed Bible warning, living licentiously in utter defiance of the laws of God as if they are answerable to nobody. As the world nears its final end, true Christians are enjoined to be sober and prayerful. (1 Peter 4:7) One who is given to sobriety will be conscious of his ways, whether in thoughts, (Acts 24:16) utterances (Proverbs 10:19, James 1:19) and actions in general (1 Corinthians 9:25-27). God Almighty Who takes account of our efforts to please Him, has assured us of his manifold blessings and protection at the end. – Hebrews 6:10; Malachi 3:17,18.

devotionals.comment:
Sin ordinarily, is the violation of God's commandments. (1 John 3:4) It incurs the wrath of God, and is evident of lack of awe for God's statutes, hence the admonition of King David: “Stand in awe, and sin not”. (Psalm 4:4).

One profound benefit we derive from God's word is, it builds faith. (Romans 10:17) Paul the Apostle wrote: “For unto us was the gospel preached, as well as unto them: but the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it.” (Hebrews 4:2) Faithlessness therefore, best explains the inconsistency of their worship to God. For every difficulty that came their way, beginning with the Red Sea ahead, Pharaoh's hosts chasing them behind, lack of food, water and fear of enemy nations, they murmured against the Almighty Father and Moses, their visible shepherd. (Numbers 21:5) As pilgrims in a sinful world, let the fear of God continue to be our guide, as we labour “to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief.” – Hebrews 4:11.

devotionals.comment:
In order that we may enjoy the rich promises awaiting the righteous in God's fully established kingdom, no sin is too pleasurable to forego, or commandment of God, difficult to keep, if we truly desire life. For one to continue in sin, and hopes to be in the kingdom of God amounts to self-deceit, hence Paul the Apostle adds: “…Be not deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor effeminate, no abusers of themselves with mankind, nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God.”

While not comparing sins, the fact remains that, both vices of adultery and fornication are highly detested before God, for which 23,000 persons died within a day, (1 Corinthians 10:8) The cities of Sodom and Gomorrha were destroyed for the sin of sodomy (Genesis 19:24) and even spiritual fornication, or mixed worship, for which 3,000 persons were destroyed in a day (Exodus 32:1-35) St. Paul enlightens us on this: “Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body.” – 1 Corinthians 6:18.

devotionals.comment:
As the dawn of each new day draws us closer to the end of this world, there is no better time to “cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light.” (Romans 13:12) Continuing in verse 13, we are warned to do away with drunkenness, among other vices, so enumerated.

Today, the vice of drunkenness is taking its toll on many, especially the youths. Virtually every achievement must be celebrated on alcoholic beverages and evening hours. Weekends and leisure hours must be spent in pubs or bars. Isaiah the prophet captures it in this wise…. “And behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen, and killing sheep, eating flesh, and drinking wine: let us eat and drink; for morrow we shall die.” (Isaiah 22:13) This should not be the attitude of those who are in the light. Paul admonished; “See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil…And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the spirit…” – Ephesians 5:15–18, 20.

devotionals.text: “And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares. For as a snare shall it come on all them that dwell on the face of the whole earth.” – Luke 21:34,35.
devotionals.comment: To take “heed” is to pay careful attention, as far as our conduct is concerned. Highlighted in Christ's admonition, among other vices, is surfeiting, an over-indulgence in something, as it has to do with food and drink, or anything negative. We cannot, having been once enlightened through warnings, exhortations, instructions, all from the Holy Bible, afford to live a care-free life, and thereby make light of the grace of God on us. To this end, St. Paul reminded us: “But ye, brethren, are not in darkness, that that day should overtake you as a thief… But let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for an helmet, the hope of salvation.” (1 Thessalonians 5:4-8) We pray God Almighty to continually help us in our determination to forsake falsehood, filthy acts, godless ways and all lusts, “with hope and faith unwavering”, by His grace. – Romans 8:13,14; Galatians 5:16.

devotionals.text: “Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul.” – 1 Peter 2:11.
devotionals.comment:
One who loves life and desires to “see good days”, should strive to both conquer and detach himself from all distractions as did Lot in his days. (2 Peter 2:8) The Holy Bible uses expressions as “works of darkness” (Romans 13:12), “unfruitful works of darkness” (Ephesians 5:11), “works of the flesh” (Galatians 5:19), etc., as synonyms for “fleshly lusts” as used by Saint Peter in the day's text.

In simple terms, these are vices, pleasures, or acts that gratify the individual, but are abhorred by God Almighty. The point is, at no time should we allow ourselves to become slave to sin, but should instead, gain control over them, with the help of God Almighty, lest they become a stumbling block in our quest for life eternal, God forbid! The above is aptly captured in Paul's exhortation when he counselled believers to “lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us.” – Hebrews 12:1.

devotionals.theme: PASSING THE TIME OF OUR SOJOURNING HERE IN FEAR
devotionals.themeIntroduction: True to scriptural prophecies pointing to the evils of this age, evil men and seducers are intensifying their acts of godlessness to such a disturbing height, with utter disregard for God's laws and human decency. As a peculiar people called to make a difference “in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation”, we are expected to shine as light, Jesus Christ admonishes us to be watchful and prayerful, while Paul the Apostle exhorts us to spiritual circumspection, “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil”. (Luke 21:36; Ephesians 5:15,16) The fear of God, thus, encompasses keeping to His ordinance, (Ecclesiastes 12:13) detaching ourselves from the ungodly and from “all-appearance of evil”. devotionals.text: “For all those things hath mine hand made, and all those things have been, saith the Lord: but to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word.” – Isaiah 66:2.
devotionals.comment:
The God of truth expressed His justified disapproval over the brazen disregard for His precepts by the unbelieving Jews, through one of His prophets, Jeremiah, thus: “Fear ye not me? Saith the LORD; will ye not tremble at my presence…? But this people hath a revolting and a rebellious heart; they are revolted and gone.” (Jeremiah 5:22, 23) To transgress the statutes of God Almighty is an act of rebellion indeed, which shows the lack of fear and reverence for Him, for which the ungodly shall not escape His anger, except they repent.

In contrast, the text for today reminds us of God's assured blessings, where we are humble enough to be under the dictate of God's word. (Job 36:11) Such act of submission is a manifestation of the fear of God, for us to gain God's favour. As we tread this woeful world, “let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear.” – Hebrews 12:28.

devotionals.text: “But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer.” – 1 Peter 4:7.
devotionals.comment: Sober-mindedness, otherwise called “sobriety”, and other allied virtues such as modesty, self-control, meekness, etc., make one to be conscious and always at alert, against the machinations of the Devil, who is now intensifying efforts to drag as many people as possible along with him into destruction. In addition to being sober-minded, we are expected to be studious, so as to be well equipped with the accurate knowledge of God's will concerning us, and being practical so as to put the truth into action. In the words of our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ, having met these standards, “ye may be accounted worthy to escape all these things that shall come to pass, and to stand before the Son of man.” (Luke 21:36) It is our prayer that God Almighty helps us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts, so as to live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world” by His grace.
